title: Amplifier classes and circuits
blurb: Explain amplifier classes, why switching amplifiers are efficient, and read the bias parts in a common-emitter circuit.

E7B01.why: Class AB conducts **more than 180° but less than 360°**. In push-pull, each device conducts a bit more than half the cycle.
E7B01.trap: Exactly 180° is Class B; the full cycle is Class A; less than 180° is Class C.

E7B02.why: Class D **switches** its device fully on and off, which keeps heat low and efficiency high.
E7B02.trap: Class D is not about linearity or distortion-free biasing; that is Class A.

E7B03.why: Switching makes square edges full of harmonics, so a **filter at the output removes harmonic content**.
E7B03.trap: A load resistor doesn't remove harmonics; it would only waste power.

E7B04.why: Class A conducts the whole cycle, so its Q-point sits **about halfway between saturation and cutoff**, leaving room to swing both ways.
E7B04.trap: Near cutoff is Class B or C; the Q-point is about the load line, not resistor values.

E7B05.why: Stray feedback causes parasitic oscillation. **Parasitic suppressors and/or neutralization** stop it.
E7B05.trap: Tuning for maximum power or minimum loading does not stop feedback oscillation.

E7B06.why: In a grounded-grid stage the signal enters at the cathode (like a transistor emitter), a **low-impedance** input.
E7B06.trap: Don't confuse it with the grounded-cathode stage, which has high input impedance.

E7B07.why: Class C conducts less than half a cycle and is nonlinear. An SSB signal's envelope gets distorted, spreading **distortion and excess bandwidth**.
E7B07.trap: Class C is efficient, not clean; it creates intermodulation instead of reducing it.

E7B08.why: Heat is V × I. A switch is **saturated (low V) or cut off (low I)** most of the time, so little power is lost.
E7B08.trap: Efficiency comes from how the device is driven, not from higher voltage or push-pull.

E7B09.why: An emitter follower (common collector) gives an output **in phase** with its input. Common emitter inverts.
E7B09.trap: Phase inversion and low input impedance belong to other configurations.

E7B10.why: R1 from the supply and R2 to ground form a **voltage divider** that sets the transistor's base bias.
E7B10.trap: They don't carry the output, so they are not load resistors, and they feed no signal back.

E7B11.why: R3 sits in the emitter leg. More current raises its voltage and reduces base drive: **self bias**.
E7B11.trap: C3 is the emitter bypass, not R3; the output load is the collector resistor.

E7B12.why: Input goes to the base, output comes off the collector, emitter is the shared leg: **common emitter**.
E7B12.trap: Emitter follower and common collector are the same circuit, with output taken at the emitter.
